books.author: Wheel of Heaven Translation Program
books.translationNote: Wheel of Heaven Translation, drafted 2026-05-18 by Claude Opus 4.7 against translation-glossary v1.0.0; source text is the Westminster Leningrad Codex (Tanach with Ta'amei Hamikra, Public Domain). Pending human review.

books.author: Wheel of Heaven Translation Program
books.translationNote: Planned Wheel of Heaven Translation from the pointed Hebrew Masoretic text (Westminster Leningrad Codex, Public Domain). Phase 2 priority per the translation roadmap; scope: chapters 1–20 initially (the liberation arc and the Sinai theophany through the Decalogue), extending later as reviewer bandwidth allows.

books.author: Wheel of Heaven Translation Program
books.translationNote: Planned Wheel of Heaven Translation from the pointed Hebrew Masoretic text (Westminster Leningrad Codex, Public Domain). Phase 1 cross-book pipeline pilot — chapter 1 first (the throne-vision, the four chayyot, the chashmal, the wheels-within-wheels), then chapters 10 and 37 (the throne-return and the valley of dry bones). Single highest-leverage chapter on the project's Hebrew Bible roadmap; the Ezekiel-as-ancient-astronaut reading is one of the most-cited associated topics.

books.author: Wheel of Heaven Translation Program
books.translationNote: Planned Wheel of Heaven Translation from the pointed Hebrew Masoretic text (Westminster Leningrad Codex, Public Domain). Phase 2 priority. Initial scope: chapter 6 (throne-room vision), chapters 24–27 (the 'Little Apocalypse'), chapter 53 (the suffering servant). Extension to other chapters deferred to reassessment.

books.author: Wheel of Heaven Translation Program
books.translationNote: Planned Wheel of Heaven Translation from the pointed Hebrew Masoretic text (Westminster Leningrad Codex, Public Domain). Phase 2 priority. Initial scope: chapters 1–2 (the bnei-elohim council scene, central to the WoH divine-council reading) and chapters 38–42 (the divine speeches with the behemoth and leviathan material). The Dhorme/RNKJV translation divergence the Raëlian canon notes is located in Job 37–38 and will surface as part of this work.

books.author: Wheel of Heaven Translation Program
books.translationNote: Planned Wheel of Heaven Translation from the polytonic Greek New Testament (Tregelles 1857–1879 edition, Public Domain). Phase 4 priority. Matthew is the most heavily cited NT book in the Raëlian canon and carries the Parable of the Sower (chapter 13) that the canon reads cosmologically.

books.author: Wheel of Heaven Translation Program
books.translationNote: Planned Wheel of Heaven Translation from the polytonic Greek New Testament (Tregelles 1857–1879 edition, Public Domain). Phase 4 priority. The Apocalypse of John is the strongest WoH-interpretive-payoff text in the New Testament — the throne-vision sequence in chapters 4–6 reads productively under the WoH lens, and the Raëlian canon engages it directly in *The New Revelations*.

books.author: Wheel of Heaven Translation Program
books.translationNote: Planned Wheel of Heaven Translation from openly-licensed Akkadian transliterations (ETCSL/CDLI/ORACC corpora; CC-BY-NC-SA where applicable). Phase 3 priority — paired with the Genesis-WoH flood narrative (chs 6–9) as the project's first cross-tradition pairing. Initial scope: Tablet XI (the flood narrative) only; expansion to other tablets is a reassessment decision.

books.author: Wheel of Heaven Translation Program
books.translationNote: Planned Wheel of Heaven Translation from the Arabic Qur'an (Tanzil.net, Uthmanic Hafs recension). Phase 3 priority — scope strictly limited to Suras 21:1–5, 54:1, and 56:15–24 (the three citations the Raëlian canon engages directly in *Extra-Terrestrials Took Me To Their Planet*). The project must engage Islam respectfully and technically; the Edition track (working from a PD English translation with the WoH glossary applied) is available as a fallback if Translation-track competence is the constraint.

books.author: Wheel of Heaven Translation Program
books.translationNote: Planned Wheel of Heaven Translation. Initial scope: the Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch chs 1–36), the most directly WoH-resonant material in the pseudepigrapha. Phase 5 priority. Source: Charles 1912 critical edition (Public Domain) as base reference; the Knibb 1978 and Nickelsburg 2001 Hermeneia editions serve as scholarly references but are copyrighted and not the ship-text. The Watchers narrative (chs 6–11) is named in the Raëlian canon's commentary section as one of the texts closer to its truth.

books.author: Wheel of Heaven Translation Program
books.translationNote: Planned Wheel of Heaven Translation. Curated selection from the Shi'ur Qomah / Hekhalot literature — the Hebrew esoteric corpus the Raëlian canon implicitly engages when it cites 'the Kabbalah' for the *parasangs*-measurement and 'height of the creator' passages (*The End of the World*, *At the Root of All Religions*). Phase 5 priority. Closing one of the genuine source-tensions named in the *Reference corpus of the Raëlian canon* wiki entry. Source text and scope to be determined at translation start; not a complete book translation.

books.author: Wheel of Heaven Translation Program
books.translationNote: Wheel of Heaven Translation from the Sumerian composite transliteration of ETCSL 1.1.2. The Sumerian human-creation text: the antediluvian lesser-gods' toil at canal-digging, Namma's lament to Enki, the grinding of clay above the abzu to create humans for divine labor, and the Enki-Ninmah contest assigning fates to defective bodies. The Mesopotamian counterpart to Genesis 1-2 on human crafting; pairs with Atraḫasīs on the humans-as-relief-of-divine-toil motif. ~141 lines.

books.author: Wheel of Heaven Translation Program
books.originalTitle: (no Sumerian title preserved; ETCSL incipit-based heading)
books.translationNote: Wheel of Heaven Translation from the Sumerian composite transliteration of ETCSL 1.7.4 (The Flood Story). The fragmentary Sumerian flood-narrative — the cleanest pre-Akkadian bridge to Genesis 6-9. Of an estimated ~262 original lines, only ~89 are preserved across 5 segments (A-E), with 4 large lacunae (~32, 34, 38, 33 lines missing) plus an opening lacuna of ~36 lines before Segment A. Ziusudra is the Sumerian flood-survivor (the *zi-ud-sura*, 'life of long days'); he is warned by Enki, builds a boat, survives a seven-day storm, sacrifices to An and Enlil, and is granted immortal life in Dilmun.

books.author: Wheel of Heaven Translation Program
books.translationNote: Wheel of Heaven Translation from the Sumerian composite transliteration of ETCSL 1.1.1. The Sumerian Dilmun paradise text — the pure land where no animal preyed and no human suffered illness; Enki's irrigation of Dilmun; the birth-sequences; the eight forbidden plants; Enki's illness in eight body-parts; Ninhursag's healing; the eight healing-deities. The text pairs with Gen 2-3 (Eden) on multiple comparative-mythology axes (paradise-as-precondition, rib/Ninti motif, forbidden-plants, paradisal healing). 256 preserved lines across 6 small in-line lacunae.
